narrative:
The model estimates a 47% chance that you will leave your current role, which is high enough for the organization to deny your promotion as a precaution against investing in someone who might soon depart.

Three factors stood out most in the model's reasoning. First, having received other job offers while at the company was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward leaving. Most employees predicted to stay had not received such external opportunities, so this signal stood out as a clear risk for turnover.

Second, the length of time you have spent in your current role worked in your favor. With 6–10 years already invested here—longer than the majority of employees the model expects to stay—this history of stability pulled the prediction back toward staying.

Third, your overall career experience of 6–10 years also nudged the outcome toward leaving. While this is fairly common, it is less typical among those the model believes will remain, suggesting you may have reached a career stage where external moves become more attractive.

Taken together, the combination of active external opportunities and your experience level outweighed the stabilizing effect of your tenure. The organization should discuss retention options with you, while you may want to reflect on whether those outside offers better match your long-term goals.
